title: Meridian Cyber — About
content:
Meridian Cyber delivers autonomous threat detection and response for the enterprise. In a world where cyberattacks move at machine speed, human-dependent security operations are no longer sufficient. Meridian changes the equation.

Our platform continuously monitors enterprise environments — endpoints, networks, cloud infrastructure, and identity systems — using AI models trained on real-world attack telemetry to detect threats with precision that surpasses traditional rule-based and signature-based approaches. When a threat is confirmed, Meridian doesn't just alert your team. It responds. Autonomously isolating compromised assets, revoking suspicious credentials, blocking lateral movement, and initiating forensic capture — all within seconds of detection.

Most security platforms detect. Meridian detects and acts.

Founded in 2022 by Rachel Kim, a 15-year veteran of the National Security Agency and enterprise cybersecurity, and Oleg Petrov, former principal engineer at Palo Alto Networks, Meridian Cyber was built on a simple conviction: the gap between detection and response is where breaches happen. Our mission is to close that gap entirely.

Meridian serves 35 enterprise customers including three Fortune 500 companies across financial services, healthcare, and critical infrastructure. Our platform processes over 2 billion security events per day across our customer base, with a median detection-to-response time of 4.2 seconds.

Based in Washington, DC, with offices in San Francisco and Tel Aviv, Meridian Cyber is backed by Bessemer Venture Partners. Our team of 65 includes threat researchers, ML engineers, and security architects drawn from the NSA, GCHQ, Unit 8200, and leading cybersecurity companies.

title: Meridian Cyber — Intro Meeting with Rachel Kim
author: Sarah Chen
content:
Meeting Type: Intro meeting (in-person, RSA Conference)
Date: May 8, 2026
Attendees: Sarah Chen (AIVC), James Morrison (AIVC), Rachel Kim (CEO, Meridian Cyber)

Context: Met Rachel at RSA Conference. She was introduced by a mutual contact (Mike Torres, CISO at JPMorgan). Had a 45-minute conversation at the event. Rachel is sharp, direct, no-nonsense — the kind of founder enterprise security buyers trust immediately.

Key Discussion Points:

- Rachel's background is exceptional. 15 years at the NSA, most recently leading a team focused on adversarial AI and automated cyber operations. She left NSA in 2022 specifically because she saw that enterprise security was stuck in a detect-and-alert paradigm while adversaries were automating their attacks. Her thesis: defense needs to be as automated as offense.

- Meridian's differentiation is autonomous response. Most competitors (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Darktrace) do AI-powered detection, but the response is still largely manual — the SOC team reviews alerts and decides what to do. Meridian's platform makes response decisions autonomously: isolating endpoints, revoking credentials, blocking network segments, all in seconds.

- This is a big technical and trust challenge. Customers need to believe the system won't take disruptive actions on false positives. Rachel's approach: a confidence-calibrated response framework. Low-confidence detections generate alerts. Medium-confidence triggers reversible containment (isolate endpoint, require MFA re-authentication). High-confidence triggers aggressive response (kill processes, revoke credentials, block lateral movement). The thresholds are configurable per customer.

- Customer traction is strong. 35 enterprise customers total, including 3 Fortune 500 (two financial services, one healthcare). Rachel mentioned a 0% logo churn rate, though the company is still young enough that this metric has limited significance.

- The numbers are impressive. Over 2B security events processed per day across the customer base. Median detection-to-response time of 4.2 seconds. Rachel cited a case study where Meridian automatically contained a ransomware attack at a financial services customer within 11 seconds of initial compromise — before the attacker could encrypt a single file.

- Team is 65 people, heavily technical. About 40% have intelligence community or military cyber backgrounds. Oleg Petrov (CTO, ex-Palo Alto Networks) was not at the conference.

Funding / Round Details:

- Raised $18M Series A from Bessemer in 2024. ARR is currently in the $8-12M range (Rachel was not specific but indicated strong growth).

- Currently raising a $45M Series B. Multiple VCs are interested — Rachel mentioned conversations with Sequoia, Accel, and Lightspeed. The round will be competitive.

- Bessemer is expected to participate in the B round. They're looking for one or two new investors to co-lead.

AIVC Fit / Concerns:

- The company is exceptional. Rachel is an outstanding founder, the product is differentiated, the market (AI security) is enormous and growing rapidly, and the customer traction is real.

- The concern is round size and our fund dynamics. $45M is a large round. Even if we participate rather than lead, the minimum allocation is likely $5-8M. For our fund size, that's a significant concentration in a single deal. We'd need high conviction.

- Valuation is expected to be $300-400M pre-money. At the top end, that's aggressive for a company at ~$10M ARR, though the growth rate and market position may justify it.

- There's a strategic question: should AIVC participate in rounds this large? Our sweet spot is leading Series A rounds at $10-20M. Participating in a $45M B round is different — less ownership, less influence, and potentially less access.

Overall Impression: This is a category-defining company in a market that is only going to get larger. Rachel Kim may be the best cybersecurity founder I've met. The question isn't whether Meridian is a great company — it is. The question is whether the round structure works for AIVC.

Action Items:
- James to research whether there's room for a smaller allocation ($3-5M) and whether that makes economic sense for our fund
- James to assess expected valuation and model returns at various ownership scenarios
- Sarah to discuss with David whether we should be expanding into larger rounds as a strategy question
- Follow up with Rachel within 2 weeks — this round will move fast

title: Meridian Cyber — Series B Round Research Memo
author: James Morrison
content:
From: James Morrison <james@aivc.com>
To: Sarah Chen <sarah@aivc.com>
Date: May 12, 2026
Subject: Meridian Cyber — Series B Round Research Memo

Hi Sarah,

Following up on the RSA meeting with Rachel Kim. I've done some digging on the round dynamics and have some findings to share.

Valuation & Round Structure:

- Market intel suggests the round will price at $300-350M pre-money, potentially higher given competitive dynamics. At $45M raised on a $350M pre, the post-money would be $395M.

- Bessemer is expected to invest $10-12M to maintain their ownership. That leaves ~$33-35M for new investors.

- Sequoia and Accel are both actively engaged. Word is that Sequoia is angling to lead at a $300M pre. Accel may be pushing to co-lead. There's reportedly also interest from IVP and Insight Partners.

- Minimum ticket for new investors is likely $5-8M. Rachel is trying to keep the cap table clean and doesn't want more than 2-3 new investors in the round.

Return Modeling:

I modeled a few scenarios for a $5M investment at a $350M pre-money:

- At a $2B exit (5.7x from post-money): our $5M returns ~$25M (5x gross)
- At a $5B exit (12.7x from post-money): our $5M returns ~$63M (12.6x gross)
- At a $10B exit (25.3x from post-money): our $5M returns ~$127M (25.3x gross)

For context, CrowdStrike peaked at ~$75B market cap. SentinelOne peaked at ~$17B. If Meridian achieves category-leader status in autonomous security, a $10B+ outcome is plausible but would require continued exceptional execution.

Competitive Landscape:

The enterprise AI security market is large ($30B+ by 2028) and growing fast. Key dynamics:

- CrowdStrike is the incumbent leader but slow to adopt autonomous response. Their platform still relies heavily on human-in-the-loop for response actions.

- SentinelOne recently acquired an AI security startup for $200M (see attached article), signaling they're moving toward autonomous response. This validates Meridian's approach but also increases competitive pressure.

- Darktrace (UK, public) has autonomous response capabilities but has faced questions about efficacy and customer retention.

- Several smaller startups are also building in this space (Vectra AI, Torq, Tines) but none have Meridian's combination of technical depth and enterprise traction.

Recommendation:

Meridian is clearly an exceptional company in one of the most attractive markets in enterprise software. The question is fit with our fund strategy.

Arguments for investing:
- Access to a category-defining company at a reasonable valuation relative to potential outcomes
- Rachel Kim is a generational founder in cybersecurity
- Strategic — gives AIVC credibility in the AI security category

Arguments against:
- $5M minimum is a large single bet for our fund
- We'd own ~1.3% of the company — limited influence
- This is a participation role, not a lead role. Doesn't build our brand the same way
- Takes capital away from Series A leads where we have more ownership and influence

I lean toward passing on this specific round but maintaining the relationship. If Meridian continues to execute, there may be opportunities to participate in later rounds or co-invest alongside Bessemer in follow-on capacity. Worth discussing with the full team.

Happy to chat through any of this.

Best,
James

title: Meridian Cyber's Autonomous Threat Response Catches Three Fortune 500 Clients
author: Steve Morgan
content:
In an industry crowded with companies promising AI-powered security, Washington DC-based Meridian Cyber is distinguishing itself with something most competitors still only aspire to: fully autonomous threat response.

The three-year-old startup, founded by former NSA cyber operations veteran Rachel Kim and ex-Palo Alto Networks engineer Oleg Petrov, has landed three Fortune 500 customers in the past six months — a velocity that has caught the attention of enterprise security leaders and investors alike.

Meridian's platform goes beyond the detection capabilities that have become standard in modern endpoint and network security tools. While most platforms flag suspicious activity and route it to a security operations center for human review, Meridian's system can autonomously execute response actions: isolating compromised endpoints, revoking credentials, blocking lateral movement, and initiating forensic preservation — all within seconds of detection.

'The average time from initial compromise to lateral movement in a modern ransomware attack is 84 minutes,' Kim told Cybersecurity Ventures. 'The average time for a SOC team to triage an alert and initiate response is 4-6 hours. That math doesn't work. By the time a human responds, the attacker has already moved. We close that gap.'

Meridian's approach relies on what Kim describes as a 'confidence-calibrated response framework.' The system assigns a confidence score to each detection and calibrates the aggressiveness of its response accordingly. Low-confidence detections generate standard alerts. Medium-confidence triggers reversible containment actions like endpoint isolation and forced re-authentication. High-confidence detections trigger aggressive response including process termination and credential revocation.

The company processes over 2 billion security events per day across its customer base and reports a median detection-to-response time of 4.2 seconds. Kim cited a recent incident at a financial services customer where the platform contained a ransomware attack within 11 seconds of initial compromise — before any files were encrypted.

Meridian raised an $18 million Series A from Bessemer Venture Partners in 2024 and has grown to 65 employees. The company is understood to be in discussions for a significantly larger Series B round.

'Rachel is building the company that the security industry has been waiting for,' said Alex Ferrara, partner at Bessemer. 'Autonomous response is the endgame in enterprise security, and Meridian is the clear leader.'

title: CrowdStrike Reports Record Q4 as Enterprise AI Security Demand Surges
author: Jordan Novet
content:
CrowdStrike reported fourth-quarter results that beat analyst estimates across the board, with annual recurring revenue growing 33% year-over-year to $3.8 billion, driven by surging enterprise demand for AI-powered security.

The cybersecurity leader posted Q4 revenue of $1.06 billion, up 35% from the year-ago quarter, with a net new ARR addition of $280 million — the largest quarterly addition in the company's history. Operating margins expanded to 23%, up from 18% a year earlier.

CEO George Kurtz attributed the strong results to accelerating enterprise adoption of AI-powered security tools in response to an increasingly sophisticated threat landscape. 'The threat actors have gone AI-native,' Kurtz said on the earnings call. 'Our customers are responding by consolidating on platforms that can detect and respond to AI-powered attacks. CrowdStrike is the platform of choice for the world's largest enterprises.'

The company highlighted the growing contribution of its Charlotte AI assistant, which uses generative AI to help security analysts investigate threats and automate routine tasks. Kurtz said Charlotte AI is now deployed at over 1,500 customers and is 'fundamentally changing the productivity of security operations.'

Analysts noted that CrowdStrike's results validate the thesis that AI security is becoming a top spending priority for enterprise CISOs. However, several pointed out that CrowdStrike's approach to AI remains largely in the 'detection and analyst augmentation' category rather than the fully autonomous response model being pursued by startups like Meridian Cyber and SentinelOne.

'CrowdStrike is delivering excellent results with an AI-assisted model,' wrote Dan Ives of Wedbush Securities. 'The question is whether the market will shift toward fully autonomous response over the next 2-3 years. If it does, CrowdStrike will need to evolve or risk ceding ground to more aggressive players.'

Shares rose 8% in after-hours trading following the report.

title: SentinelOne Acquires AI Security Startup for $200M to Bolster Autonomous Response
author: Carly Page
content:
SentinelOne, the cybersecurity company known for its AI-powered endpoint protection platform, has acquired Arktose Security, a startup specializing in autonomous incident response orchestration, for approximately $200 million in a mix of cash and stock.

The acquisition signals SentinelOne's intent to compete more directly with Meridian Cyber and other startups building fully autonomous security response capabilities — a category that has attracted significant investor interest amid growing concern about the speed and sophistication of AI-powered cyberattacks.

Arktose, a 40-person startup based in Austin, Texas, built a platform that integrates with existing security tools to automate response workflows without human intervention. The technology uses reinforcement learning to optimize response actions based on the specific characteristics of each threat, the criticality of affected assets, and the organization's risk tolerance.

'The security industry has spent two decades getting really good at detection,' said Tomer Weingarten, CEO of SentinelOne. 'But detection without response is just a more sophisticated way of telling you that you're being breached. The next frontier is closing the loop — detecting and responding in real time, at machine speed, without waiting for a human to make the call.'

The acquisition will be integrated into SentinelOne's Singularity platform, which already includes AI-powered threat detection across endpoints, cloud, and identity. The addition of Arktose's autonomous response capabilities positions SentinelOne to compete more directly with Meridian Cyber, the Washington DC-based startup that has attracted attention for its fully autonomous threat response platform.

Meridian Cyber CEO Rachel Kim, a former NSA veteran, has been vocal about the need for autonomous response, arguing that human-dependent security operations cannot keep pace with automated attacks. SentinelOne's move to acquire response automation capabilities appears to validate this thesis.

Analysts at Forrester Research described the acquisition as 'inevitable.' 'Every major security platform will need autonomous response capabilities within the next 2-3 years,' wrote Forrester analyst Allie Mellen. 'The question is build vs. buy, and SentinelOne has chosen to buy. That likely accelerates the timeline for the entire industry.'

SentinelOne shares rose 5% on the news. Meridian Cyber, which is privately held and understood to be raising a Series B, declined to comment.
